messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step outline of how you could use the two tools you described to place an order for a burger and fries at McDonald’s. I’ll keep it high‑level so you can adapt it to whatever concrete APIs or SDKs you end up finding. --- ## 1. Search the Internet for Relevant API Calls | What you do | Why it matters | |-------------|----------------| | **Invoke the “search” tool** with a query such as:
`“McDonald’s online ordering API”`
`“McDonald’s menu JSON”`
`“McDonald’s order placement endpoint”` | You need to discover the public or partner‑only endpoints that let you fetch the menu, add items to a cart, and submit an order. | | **Collect the URLs and documentation snippets** returned by the search. | These will tell you the exact HTTP method, required headers, query parameters, and payload structure. | | **Identify any authentication mechanism** (OAuth2, API key, JWT, etc.) that the McDonald’s API requires. | Without proper auth you won’t be able to place an order. | > **Tip:** If the search returns a “McDonald’s Developer Portal” or a “Partner API” link, that’s usually the most reliable source. --- ## 2. Resolve the Menu Items (Burger & Fries) | What you do | Why it matters | |-------------|----------------| | **Call the “execute API” tool** to hit the menu endpoint you found, e.g.:
`GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu?location=12345` | You need the real product IDs for the burger and fries you want to order. | | **Parse the JSON response** to locate the specific items (e.g., “Big Mac” and “Large French Fries”). | The order payload will reference these IDs, not the human‑readable names. | | **Store the item IDs** (and any required modifiers like size or toppings). | These IDs will be inserted into the order payload later. | --- ## 3. Build the Order Payload | What you do | Why it matters | |-------------|----------------| | **Create a JSON object** that follows the schema the ordering endpoint expects. A typical payload looks like: | You need to match the exact field names and nesting required by the API. | | ```json
{
"location_id": "12345",
"items": [
{ "product_id": "burger_001", "quantity": 1 },
{ "product_id": "fries_002", "quantity": 1 }
],
"payment_method": { "type": "card", "token": "abc123" },
"delivery_address": { "street": "...", "city": "...", "zip": "..." }
}
``` | Replace the placeholders with the real IDs, payment token, and address you want to use. | | **Add any optional fields** (promo codes, special instructions, pickup vs delivery). | Some APIs require these for a successful order. | --- ## 4. Authenticate (If Needed) | What you do | Why it matters | |-------------|----------------| | **Obtain an access token** if the API uses OAuth2 or similar. This might involve:
• Calling a token endpoint with client credentials
• Using a pre‑existing token from a user login flow | The token will be sent in the `Authorization` header of your order request. | | **Include the token** in the headers of the order request:
`Authorization: Bearer ` | Without this header the API will reject the request. | --- ## 5. Execute the Order | What you do | Why it matters | |-------------|----------------| | **Call the “execute API” tool** with the order endpoint, e.g.:
`POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders`
Headers: `{"Content-Type":"application/json","Authorization":"Bearer "}`
Body: *the JSON payload you built* | This is the actual “place order” call. | | **Check the response** for success status (200‑299) and any order confirmation details (order ID, ETA). | You’ll need this to confirm the order was accepted and to track it later. | --- ## 6. Handle Errors & Retries | What you do | Why it matters | |-------------|----------------| | **Inspect the HTTP status code** and error message. Common issues:
• 401/403 – bad/missing auth
• 404 – wrong endpoint
• 422 – invalid payload
• 429 – rate limiting | Knowing the error lets you correct the request or back‑off. | | **Retry with exponential back‑off** if you hit transient errors (429, 503). | Avoid hammering the API and improve reliability. | --- ## 7. Confirm & Track the Order | What you do | Why it matters | |-------------|----------------| | **Use the order ID** returned in the response to poll a “status” endpoint, e.g.:
`GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders//status` | Lets you know when the order is being prepared, out for delivery, or completed. | | **Optionally set up a webhook** if the API supports it, so you’re notified automatically when the status changes. | Reduces polling overhead and gives real‑time updates. | --- ## 8. Wrap Up 1. **Search** → Find the right endpoints and docs. 2. **Resolve** → Get the product IDs for burger & fries. 3. **Build** → Construct the order JSON. 4. **Auth** → Get a bearer token or other auth header. 5. **Execute** → POST the order. 6. **Handle** → Deal with errors & retries. 7. **Track** → Poll or subscribe to status updates. Once you’ve gone through these steps, you’ll have a fully functional “order a burger and fries” workflow that can be automated or integrated into a larger system.
